seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the six claims gain a second author: that staying alive is not the great thing, that the soul is the measure and fame is not, that being just is enough, and the wide view. The article gains a way to look at a person stripped of everything but the soul, a model to live by, birth set beside fame and power, the names of what the conquerors were slaves to, justice without renown, and the duty to stay alive for those who need me. He limits one claim: for him the glory of a death proves nothing, but how a person meets death does judge a soul.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a method: to see the soul I set aside, in my mind, the estate, the titles and even the body. He limits the claim behind “not by fame”: the glory of a death does not count for him either, but how a person meets death does.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: mere living is not a good, but living well
piece.follows: Merely being alive is not a good; living well is.
piece.context: Letter 70, on when a wise man may end his own life: life is a voyage whose harbour is death, and one should not cling to it at any price.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: It is not an important matter to live; all your slaves live, and so do all animals; but it is important to die honourably, sensibly, bravely.
piece.follows: Living is no great matter, since slaves and animals live too; what matters is to die honourably, sensibly and bravely.
piece.context: A Stoic friend is advising Marcellinus, who is ill and weighing whether to end his life. Seneca reports this as the best advice Marcellinus was given.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Consider his soul, its quality and its stature
piece.follows: To know a man, consider his soul: what it is like and how great it is.
piece.context: Seneca says we misjudge people by adding their trappings to them. “His” is any man whose true worth I want to know, once estate, titles and body are set aside.
gives: I measure a person by the kind of soul they have

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness
piece.follows: How many people know of my uprightness makes no difference.
piece.context: The close of Letter 113, on being just for its own sake: those who want their virtue advertised are after renown, not virtue. “Your uprightness” is Lucilius’s.
gives: it is not fame

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: It should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation; it should satisfy itself.
piece.follows: Justice should have nothing to do with ambition or reputation; it should be satisfied with itself.
piece.context: Seneca turns from a quibble about the virtues to what they should teach him. “It” is Justice, which looks to another’s good and seeks nothing for itself.
gives: Being just is enough for me

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: how closely in accord with nature it is to let one’s mind reach out into the boundless universe
piece.follows: It is in accord with nature to let the mind reach out into the boundless universe.
piece.context: Seneca leaves a logical quibble about fame after death and turns to the greatness of the human soul, which accepts no limit of place or of time.
gives: I take the wide view

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: no epoch is closed to great minds; all Time is open for the progress of thought
piece.follows: No age is closed to a great mind; all of time is open to thought.
piece.context: In Letter 102 Seneca lets the soul speak for itself: it will not put up with a narrow span of existence and claims all the years as its own.
gives: I take the wide view

items.label: practice
items.t: When I want to know what a person is truly worth, I look at them stripped: in my mind I set aside the estate they inherited, their titles and fortune’s other deceptions, and even the body. Otherwise I am measuring the pedestal along with the person, and a dwarf is not tall for standing on a mountain-top.
items.why: Marcus says what to look at, the soul, and the article sums up what he sets aside as fame and power. He gives no way of looking. Seneca gives one, and it sets aside more: inheritance, titles and the body itself. “Otherwise” is the editor’s join: in Letter 76 the pedestal (76.31) comes just before the stripping (76.32). “In my mind” is the editor’s: Seneca’s “naked” is a figure for setting fortune’s gifts aside in judging.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: when you wish to inquire into a man’s true worth, and to know what manner of man he is, look at him when he is naked; make him lay aside his inherited estate, his titles, and the other deceptions of fortune; let him even strip off his body
support.follows: To learn a man’s true worth, look at him without his estate, his titles, fortune’s other gifts and even his body.
support.context: Letter 76 argues that the honourable is the only good. Here Seneca gives a way to learn a man’s true worth; “naked” means without what fortune has lent him.
gives: When I want to know what a person is truly worth, I look at them stripped: in my mind I set aside the estate they inherited, their titles and fortune’s other deceptions, and even the body

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is because you are measuring the pedestal along with the man. A dwarf is not tall, though he stand upon a mountain-top
support.follows: A man raised high seems great because the pedestal is measured with him; a dwarf on a mountain-top is still not tall.
support.context: Seneca asks why those raised high by riches and honours seem great to Lucilius. The “pedestal” is the wealth and office such a man stands on.
gives: I am measuring the pedestal along with the person, and a dwarf is not tall for standing on a mountain-top

items.label: practice
items.t: I choose someone whose life and talk have satisfied me and picture that person always as my pattern, for what is crooked cannot be straightened without a ruler. If I want a pattern, I can take Socrates.
items.why: The section is Marcus’s own gallery of models, Socrates first, but no passage in it says to choose a model and keep him in view. Seneca states the practice and names the same man. He recommends Socrates for his endurance, which is part of what 7.37 says is not enough to judge him by.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Choose a master whose life, conversation, and soul-expressing face have satisfied you; picture him always to yourself as your protector or your pattern.
support.follows: I should choose a person whose life and talk satisfy me and keep him before me as my protector or pattern.
support.context: Seneca ends Letter 11 with a saying of Epicurus: keep a man of high character before your eyes. He suggests Cato or Laelius; “master” means such a model.
gives: I choose someone whose life and talk have satisfied me and picture that person always as my pattern

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you can never straighten that which is crooked unless you use a ruler
support.follows: What is crooked can be straightened only against a ruler.
support.context: The last sentence of Letter 11, giving the reason for choosing a model: we need someone by whom to regulate our characters. The “ruler” is that person.
gives: what is crooked cannot be straightened without a ruler

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If, however, you desire a pattern, take Socrates
support.follows: Anyone who wants a pattern can take Socrates.
support.context: In Letter 104 Seneca offers Lucilius a pattern and goes on to recount Socrates’ poverty, soldiering, harsh home, the Thirty Tyrants, his trial and the poison.
gives: If I want a pattern, I can take Socrates

items.label: why
items.t: Birth is not the measure either. Socrates was no aristocrat, and a hall full of ancestors’ busts does not make anyone noble: the soul alone does that, whatever condition a person started from.
items.why: The article sums up what Marcus sets aside as fame and power, and in 1.8 he notes that patricians tend to lack affection, but no passage of the section says that birth is not the measure. Seneca says it, and gives the word “noble” to the soul. The first sentence, “Birth is not the measure either”, is the editor’s summary of the three quotes and is backed by none alone.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Socrates was no aristocrat.
support.follows: Socrates was not of noble birth.
support.context: Letter 44 tells Lucilius, a Roman knight, that a noble mind is open to everyone and philosophy asks no pedigree. Socrates heads a list of philosophers of humble origin.
gives: Socrates was no aristocrat

support.author: seneca
support.quote: A hall full of smoke-begrimed busts does not make the nobleman.
support.follows: A hall full of old busts does not make a man noble.
support.context: Seneca asks who is well-born and answers: whoever is by nature fitted for virtue. The busts are the ancestor portraits kept in the hall of a noble Roman house.
gives: a hall full of ancestors’ busts does not make anyone noble

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the soul alone renders us noble, and it may rise superior to Fortune out of any earlier condition
support.follows: Only the soul makes us noble, and it can rise above fortune from any starting condition.
support.context: From Seneca’s letter on pedigrees: no life lived before ours lends us glory. “Noble” is the word for high birth, which he gives to the soul instead.
gives: the soul alone does that, whatever condition a person started from

items.label: action
items.t: I must be just without reward and without renown. Often I shall have to be just and be ill spoken of at the same time.
items.why: 7.26 and 7.37 say that being just is enough; neither says it may cost me my good name. Seneca names that cost: no reward, no renown, and often ill repute. His “disgraced” means ill spoken of. It is not the disgrace of 7.26, which is the shame of doing wrong, so the two do not conflict.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let each man convince himself of this before all else—“I must be just without reward.”
support.follows: Before anything else each person should be convinced that he must be just without reward.
support.context: The end of Letter 113, where Seneca says what Justice should teach him: it looks to another’s good and seeks nothing for itself. “Each man” includes himself.
gives: I must be just without reward

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced.
support.follows: I should be willing to be just without renown, and shall often have to be just and disgraced at once.
support.context: Seneca’s last words to Lucilius in Letter 113. “Disgraced” here means ill spoken of: the next sentence calls it ill repute, well won, and a delight to the wise.
gives: without renown
Often I shall have to be just and be ill spoken of at the same time

items.label: action
items.t: I live as long as I ought, not merely as long as it pleases me. Sometimes I must hold on to life, even at the price of great suffering, for the sake of the people I hold dear.
items.why: 7.26 tells me to let go of how long I live and leaves the length to god. Seneca, who elsewhere lets a wise man choose his hour (Letter 70), here gives the duty to stay for those who need me; only that half is used, since choosing one’s hour runs against 7.26.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the good man should not live as long as it pleases him, but as long as he ought
support.follows: A good man should live as long as he ought, not as long as it pleases him.
support.context: Seneca, old and ill, says he looks after his health for the sake of his wife Paulina, whose life hangs on his. “Ought” here means for those who need him.
gives: I live as long as I ought, not merely as long as it pleases me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the breath of life must be called back and kept at our very lips even at the price of great suffering, for the sake of those whom we hold dear
support.follows: Sometimes life must be held on to, even at the price of great suffering, for the sake of those we hold dear.
support.context: From Letter 104, where Seneca explains why he nurses his health: his wife Paulina asks it. To persist in dying when dear ones need him he calls self-indulgence.
gives: Sometimes I must hold on to life, even at the price of great suffering, for the sake of the people I hold dear

items.label: breaks
items.t: A free person can be a slave: one to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and everyone to fear. The conquerors were conquered first, by their own greed, and while they seemed to be hounding others they were themselves hounded: Alexander by a mad desire to lay waste other people’s land, Pompey by a craving for glory, Caesar by the wish to stand above everyone.
items.why: 8.3 exclaims “slavery to how many!” and does not say to what. Seneca takes the same three men, Alexander, Pompey and Gaius Caesar, and names what drove each. In Letter 94 his words are “conquered” and “hounded”; the word “slave” for such masters is from Letter 47.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Show me a man who is not a slave; one is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and all men are slaves to fear.
support.follows: No one is free of slavery: one serves lust, another greed, another ambition, and all serve fear.
support.context: Letter 47 asks Lucilius to treat his slaves as people. To the objection “He is a slave” Seneca answers that free men have masters of their own.
gives: A free person can be a slave: one to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and everyone to fear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: even these men, before they could conquer their foe, were conquered by their own greed
support.follows: Before they conquered their enemies, these men were conquered by their own greed.
support.context: Seneca describes the voice that should warn us against envying those the people call great. “These men” are generals who storm cities and reach the sea in blood.
gives: The conquerors were conquered first, by their own greed

support.author: seneca
support.quote: they themselves could not withstand desire for power and the impulse to cruelty; at the time when they seemed to be hounding others, they were themselves being hounded
support.follows: They could not withstand their own desire for power and cruelty; while they seemed to drive others, they were driven themselves.
support.context: In Letter 94, of generals who sack cities and whose attack no one withstood. “They” are these conquerors, the men the people call great and fortunate.
gives: while they seemed to be hounding others they were themselves hounded

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Alexander was hounded into misfortune and dispatched to unknown countries by a mad desire to lay waste other men’s territory.
support.follows: Alexander was driven into misfortune and into unknown lands by a mad desire to lay waste what belonged to others.
support.context: The first of Seneca’s examples in Letter 94 of men the crowd calls great who were driven, not driving. He goes on to Alexander’s ruin of Greece.
gives: Alexander by a mad desire to lay waste other people’s land

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It was not virtue or reason which persuaded Gnaeus Pompeius to take part in foreign and civil warfare; it was his mad craving for unreal glory.
support.follows: What took Pompey into his wars was not virtue or reason but a mad craving for unreal glory.
support.context: Seneca’s second example, after Alexander, of a conqueror driven by his own craving. He calls Pompey’s campaigns pretexts for extending his power.
gives: Pompey by a craving for glory

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And what impelled Gaius Caesar to the combined ruin of himself and of the state? Renown, self-seeking, and the setting no limit to pre-eminence over all other men.
support.follows: What drove Gaius Caesar to ruin himself and the state was renown, self-seeking and a limitless wish to stand above all others.
support.context: Seneca’s third example in Letter 94 of a great man driven by his own desires. This Gaius Caesar is Julius Caesar, who could not let anyone outrank him.
gives: Caesar by the wish to stand above everyone

items.t: Seneca agrees that fame is not the measure and that talk proves nothing about a soul: in Letter 26 he sets the opinion of the world aside. Marcus says that the glory of a death, how it was seen by others, is not enough to show that Socrates was the better man. Seneca says that how one meets death is the final proof of a soul’s real strength: what a person has done shows only at the last breath. He says this to himself and then to Lucilius; applying it to any soul is the editor’s step. He reads Socrates in the same way, from his trials, which did not change his soul (Ep. 104.28). He also trusts that virtue comes to light in the end, though he adds that being hidden is no loss to it (Ep. 79.17); Marcus leaves open that the better man may be one nobody knows. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: for both the soul is the measure; Marcus sets aside the glory of a death, and Seneca looks to the conduct in it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Death will deliver the final judgment in your case.
support.follows: It is death that will give the final judgment on me.
support.context: Seneca, in old age, tells himself that his words so far prove nothing about him. “Your case” is his own, and he then offers the same words to Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What you have done in the past will be manifest only at the time when you draw your last breath.
support.follows: What I have really done will be plain only when I draw my last breath.
support.context: From Letter 26, on old age and death: debates and learned talk give no proof of a soul’s real strength. “You” is Seneca addressing himself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But all these measures changed the soul of Socrates so little that they did not even change his features.
support.follows: Everything done to Socrates changed his soul so little that it did not even change his face.
support.context: Seneca’s portrait of Socrates as a pattern. “These measures” are the long war, the Thirty Tyrants, the charges against him, the prison and the cup of poison.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Virtue is never lost to view; and yet to have been lost to view is no loss. There will come a day which will reveal her
support.follows: Virtue does not stay hidden, and being hidden costs it nothing; a day will come that reveals it.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius that fame follows virtue like a shadow, sometimes late: Democritus, Socrates and Cato were recognised slowly. “Her” is virtue.

passages.title: On the proper time to slip the cable
passages.text: You may consider that the same thing happens to us: life has carried some men with the greatest rapidity to the harbour, the harbour they were bound to reach even if they tarried on the way, while others it has fretted and harassed. To such a life, as you are aware, one should not always cling. For mere living is not a good, but living well. Accordingly, the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.

passages.title: On taking one’s own life
passages.text: but our Stoic friend, a rare man, and, to praise him in language which he deserves, a man of courage and vigour admonished him best of all, as it seems to me. For he began as follows: “Do not torment yourself, my dear Marcellinus, as if the question which you are weighing were a matter of importance. It is not an important matter to live; all your slaves live, and so do all animals; but it is important to die honourably, sensibly, bravely. Reflect how long you have been doing the same thing: food, sleep, lust,—this is one’s daily round. The desire to die may be felt, not only by the sensible man or the brave or unhappy man, but even by the man who is merely surfeited.”

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: This is the error under which we labour; this is the reason why we are imposed upon: we value no man at what he is, but add to the man himself the trappings in which he is clothed. But when you wish to inquire into a man’s true worth, and to know what manner of man he is, look at him when he is naked; make him lay aside his inherited estate, his titles, and the other deceptions of fortune; let him even strip off his body. Consider his soul, its quality and its stature, and thus learn whether its greatness is borrowed, or its own.

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Fasten deep in your mind that which I remarked a short space above: that it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness. Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown. Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced. And then, if you are wise, let ill repute, well won, be a delight. Farewell.

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Self-Command is the greatest command of all. Let her teach me what a hallowed thing is the Justice which ever regards another’s good and seeks nothing for itself except its own employment. It should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation; it should satisfy itself. Let each man convince himself of this before all else—“I must be just without reward.” And that is not enough; let him convince himself also of this: “May I take pleasure in devoting myself of my own free will to uphold this noblest of virtues.” Let all his thoughts be turned as far as possible from personal interests. You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.

passages.title: On the intimations of our immortality
passages.text: Tell me rather how closely in accord with nature it is to let one’s mind reach out into the boundless universe! The human soul is a great and noble thing; it permits of no limits except those which can be shared even by the gods. First of all, it does not consent to a lowly birthplace, like Ephesus or Alexandria, or any land that is even more thickly populated than these, and more richly spread with dwellings. The soul’s homeland is the whole space that encircles the, height and breadth of the firmament, the whole rounded dome within which lie land and sea, within which the upper air that sunders the human from the divine also unites them, and where all the sentinel stars are taking their turn on duty.

passages.title: On the intimations of our immortality
passages.text: Again, the soul will not put up with a narrow span of existence. “All the years,” says the soul, “are mine; no epoch is closed to great minds; all Time is open for the progress of thought. When the day comes to separate the heavenly from its earthly blend, I shall leave the body here where I found it, and shall of my own volition betake myself to the gods. I am not apart from them now, but am merely detained in a heavy and earthly prison.”

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: None of those whom you behold clad in purple is happy, any more than one of these actors upon whom the play bestows a sceptre and a cloak while on the stage; they strut their hour before a crowded house, with swelling port and buskined foot; but when once they make their exit the foot-gear is removed and they return to their proper stature. None of those who have been raised to a loftier height by riches and honours is really great. Why then does he seem great to you? It is because you are measuring the pedestal along with the man. A dwarf is not tall, though he stand upon a mountain-top; a colossal statue will still be tall, though you place it in a well.

passages.title: On the blush of modesty
passages.text: Choose therefore a Cato; or, if Cato seems too severe a model, choose some Laelius, a gentler spirit. Choose a master whose life, conversation, and soul-expressing face have satisfied you; picture him always to yourself as your protector or your pattern. For we must indeed have someone according to whom we may regulate our characters; you can never straighten that which is crooked unless you use a ruler. Farewell.

passages.title: On care of health and peace of mind
passages.text: If, however, you desire a pattern, take Socrates, a long-suffering old man, who was sea-tossed amid every hardship and yet was unconquered both by poverty (which his troubles at home made more burdensome) and by toil, including the drudgery of military service. He was much tried at home, whether we think of his wife, a woman of rough manners and shrewish tongue, or of the children whose intractability showed them to be more like their mother than their father. And if you consider the facts, he lived either in time of war, or under tyrants, or under a democracy, which is more cruel than wars and tyrants.

passages.title: On philosophy and pedigrees
passages.text: Socrates was no aristocrat. Cleanthes worked at a well and served as a hired man watering a garden. Philosophy did not find Plato already a nobleman; it made him one. Why then should you despair of becoming able to rank with men like these? They are all your ancestors, if you conduct yourself in a manner worthy of them; and you will do so if you convince yourself at the outset that no man outdoes you in real nobility.

passages.title: On philosophy and pedigrees
passages.text: Then who is well-born? He who is by nature well fitted for virtue. That is the one point to be considered; otherwise, if you hark back to antiquity, every one traces back to a date before which there is nothing. From the earliest beginnings of the universe to the present time, we have been led forward out of origins that were alternately illustrious and ignoble. A hall full of smoke-begrimed busts does not make the nobleman. No past life has been lived to lend us glory, and that which has existed before us is not ours; the soul alone renders us noble, and it may rise superior to Fortune out of any earlier condition, no matter what that condition has been.

passages.title: On care of health and peace of mind
passages.text: For one must indulge genuine emotions; sometimes, even in spite of weighty reasons, the breath of life must be called back and kept at our very lips even at the price of great suffering, for the sake of those whom we hold dear; because the good man should not live as long as it pleases him, but as long as he ought. He who does not value his wife, or his friend, highly enough to linger longer in life—he who obstinately persists in dying—is a voluptuary. The soul should also enforce this command upon itself whenever the needs of one’s relatives require; it should pause and humour those near and dear, not only when it desires, but even when it has begun, to die.

passages.title: On master and slave
passages.text: “He is a slave.” His soul, however, may be that of a freeman. “He is a slave.” But shall that stand in his way? Show me a man who is not a slave; one is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and all men are slaves to fear. I will name you an ex-consul who is slave to an old hag, a millionaire who is slave to a serving-maid; I will show you youths of the noblest birth in serfdom to pantomime players! No servitude is more disgraceful than that which is self-imposed. You should therefore not be deterred by these finicky persons from showing yourself to your slaves as an affable person and not proudly superior to them; they ought to respect you rather than fear you.

passages.title: On the value of advice [ 1 ]
passages.text: There are many who set fire to cities, who storm garrisons that have remained impregnable for generations and safe for numerous ages, who raise mounds as high as the walls they are besieging, who with battering-rams and engines shatter towers that have been reared to a wondrous height. There are many who can send their columns ahead and press destructively upon the rear of the foe, who can reach the Great Sea dripping with the blood of nations; but even these men, before they could conquer their foe, were conquered by their own greed. No one withstood their attack; but they themselves could not withstand desire for power and the impulse to cruelty; at the time when they seemed to be hounding others, they were themselves being hounded.

passages.title: On the value of advice [ 1 ]
passages.text: Alexander was hounded into misfortune and dispatched to unknown countries by a mad desire to lay waste other men’s territory. Do you believe that the man was in his senses who could begin by devastating Greece, the land where he received his education? One who snatched away the dearest guerdon of each nation, bidding Spartans be slaves, and Athenians hold their tongues? Not content with the ruin of all the states which Philip had either conquered or bribed into bondage, he overthrew various commonwealths in various places and carried his weapons all over the world; his cruelty was tired, but it never ceased—like a wild beast that tears to pieces more than its hunger demands.

passages.title: On the value of advice [ 1 ]
passages.text: It was not virtue or reason which persuaded Gnaeus Pompeius to take part in foreign and civil warfare; it was his mad craving for unreal glory. Now he attacked Spain and the faction of Sertorius; now he fared forth to enchain the pirates and subdue the seas. These were merely excuses and pretexts for extending his power.

passages.title: On the value of advice [ 1 ]
passages.text: What drew him into Africa, into the North, against Mithridates, into Armenia and all the corners of Asia? Assuredly it was his boundless desire to grow bigger; for only in his own eyes was he not great enough. And what impelled Gaius Caesar to the combined ruin of himself and of the state? Renown, self-seeking, and the setting no limit to pre-eminence over all other men. He could not allow a single person to outrank him, although the state allowed two men to stand at its head.

passages.title: On old age and death
passages.text: Put aside the opinion of the world; it is always wavering and always takes both sides. Put aside the studies which you have pursued throughout your life; Death will deliver the final judgment in your case. This is what I mean: your debates and learned talks, your maxims gathered from the teachings of the wise, your cultured conversation,—all these afford no proof of the real strength of your soul. Even the most timid man can deliver a bold speech. What you have done in the past will be manifest only at the time when you draw your last breath. I accept the terms; I do not shrink from the decision.”

passages.title: On care of health and peace of mind
passages.text: The war lasted for twenty-seven years; then the state became the victim of the Thirty Tyrants, of whom many were his personal enemies. At the last came that climax of condemnation under the gravest of charges: they accused him of disturbing the state religion and corrupting the youth, for they declared that he had influenced the youth to defy the gods, to defy the council, and to defy the state in general. Next came the prison, and the cup of poison. But all these measures changed the soul of Socrates so little that they did not even change his features. What wonderful and rare distinction! He maintained this attitude up to the very end, and no man ever saw Socrates too much elated or too much depressed. Amid all the disturbance of Fortune, he was undisturbed.

passages.title: On the rewards of scientific discovery
passages.text: Virtue is never lost to view; and yet to have been lost to view is no loss. There will come a day which will reveal her, though hidden away or suppressed by the spite of her contemporaries. That man is born merely for a few, who thinks only of the people of his own generation. Many thousands of years and many thousands of peoples will come after you; it is to these that you should have regard. Malice may have imposed silence upon the mouths of all who were alive in your day; but there will come men who will judge you without prejudice and without favour. If there is any reward that virtue receives at the hands of fame, not even this can pass away. We ourselves, indeed, shall not be affected by the talk of posterity; nevertheless, posterity will cherish and celebrate us even though we are not conscious thereof.

claims.t: Staying alive is not the great thing, and dying is not the worst thing. Where I have taken up a post I stay and run the risk, and I weigh nothing, not even death, against doing what is shameful.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of life and of death and give neither the first place. In 7.26 Socrates asks the other man to see whether what is noble and good “may not be something other” than “saving and being saved”, and says that “neither death nor anything else” counts ahead of disgrace. In 7.23 human life does not seem “anything great”, and death is “nothing terrible”.
claims.changed: 7.26 is about a man at his post and 7.23 about a mind that has all of time in view; the claim keeps the two judgments they share and adds the post from 7.26 alone. “Dying is not the worst thing” is the least that both say: 7.26 puts disgrace ahead of death, and 7.23 goes further and calls death nothing terrible. 7.26’s third paragraph is hedged (“see whether … may not be”, “perhaps”); the article reads the hedge as Socrates’ polite way of asserting. “Dying is not the worst thing” rests on 7.26b and 7.23a, which are not hedged; “staying alive is not the great thing” rests on the hedged 7.26c and on 7.23b, which says it only of a mind with a view of all time, a condition the claim drops (see the decisions). “Doing what is shameful” follows the translators’ other reading of 7.26’s “ahead of disgrace” (Greek “before the shameful”): the disgrace meant is the shameful act, not the loss of a good name.

support.quote: see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life
support.follows: What is noble and good may be something other than staying alive, and perhaps a true man must let go of how long he lives.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

support.quote: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said.
support.follows: To the one this question is about, human life cannot seem anything great.
gives: Staying alive is not the great thing

support.quote: Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace
support.follows: Whoever has taken up a post, or been posted there, must stay and run the risk, counting nothing, death included, ahead of disgrace.
gives: dying is not the worst thing
Where I have taken up a post I stay and run the risk, and I weigh nothing, not even death, against doing what is shameful

support.quote: such a person will count death, too, as nothing terrible
support.follows: Such a person will not count death as anything terrible.

claims.t: I measure a person by the kind of soul they have. It is not power that counts: Alexander, Gaius Caesar and Pompey are little beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates. And it is not fame: for all I know, Telauges was a better man than Socrates, though hardly anyone has heard of him. Not even Socrates’ more glorious death is enough to show which of the two was better.
claims.shared: 7.37 and 8.3 both set Socrates beside other men and both look inside for the difference: 7.37 at “what kind of soul Socrates had”, 8.3 at the philosophers’ “ruling parts”. In both, what the world saw of a man is not what decides: Socrates’ glorious death in 7.37, the three conquerors in 8.3.
claims.changed: “I measure” is the editor’s word for 7.37’s “what has to be looked at” and 8.3’s “what are they beside”. 8.3 says “ruling parts”, the part of the soul that governs; the claim says “soul”, 7.37’s word. The text of 8.3’s “their ruling parts were the same” is probably doubted, but the claim uses it only to say that 8.3 looks inside the men, which holds on either reading. The Greek of 8.3 has only “Gaius”; the translators’ note says he is Gaius Julius Caesar, and the claim writes “Gaius Caesar” so that he is not taken for the emperor Caligula. Neither “fame” nor “power” is a word of the passages: “fame” sums up 7.37’s list of what was seen and told of Socrates, “power” what Alexander, Gaius and Pompey have in common.

inferences.words: though hardly anyone has heard of him
inferences.why: 7.37 names Telauges and says nothing about him. The gloss is the editor’s, from the translators’ note that he stands for a man of whom little is known.

support.quote: what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had
support.follows: The thing to look at in Socrates is what kind of soul he had.
gives: I measure a person by the kind of soul they have

support.quote: For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same.
support.follows: The reason given for setting the philosophers higher is what they saw and the state of their ruling parts.
gives: by the kind of soul they have

support.quote: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates?
support.follows: Alexander, Gaius and Pompey amount to little when set beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates.
gives: It is not power that counts: Alexander, Gaius Caesar and Pompey are little beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates

support.quote: it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists
support.follows: A more glorious death and more skill in argument are not enough to show that Socrates was the better man.
gives: it is not fame
Not even Socrates’ more glorious death is enough to show which of the two was better

support.quote: How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition?
support.follows: We do not know that Telauges was not the better man in his inner disposition.
gives: for all I know, Telauges was a better man than Socrates

claims.t: Being just is enough for me: when I act I look at this alone, whether what I am doing is just or unjust, and I ask no more of myself than to be just in my dealings with people and devout in my dealings with the gods.
claims.shared: Both passages name being just, and both say that nothing more is needed: 7.26 tells a man to “look at this alone”, whether what he does is “just or unjust”; 7.37 asks whether Socrates could “find it enough to be just”.
claims.changed: 7.26 is Socrates speaking of any man who is of use; 7.37 is a question about Socrates, not a statement. The claim says “I” and turns the question into a resolve. 7.37 puts being devout toward the gods beside being just toward people; the claim keeps it, although 7.26 does not say it.

support.quote: look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one
support.follows: Whenever a man acts he should look at one thing only: whether what he is doing is just or unjust.
gives: Being just is enough for me
when I act I look at this alone, whether what I am doing is just or unjust
I ask no more of myself than to be just

support.quote: whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods
support.follows: The question about Socrates is whether being just to people and devout to the gods was enough for him.
gives: Being just is enough for me
I ask no more of myself than to be just in my dealings with people and devout in my dealings with the gods

claims.t: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong: I do not get idly angry at vice, and I do not fight and fall out with them.
claims.shared: 7.37 and 1.7 both meet another person’s fault and both refuse the hostile answer: 7.37 has “neither getting idly angry at vice”, 1.7 “not to pounce reproachfully” on someone’s mistake. 11.32 asks people who say their souls are sound why they “fight and fall out”. The three have no word in common; what they share is the refusal.
claims.changed: 1.7 is about slips in speech and 7.37 about vice; the claim covers anything a person gets wrong. “I do not turn on people” is the editor’s summary of the two. 11.32 says nothing about faults and backs only the last words. 11.32 is a question put to people who quarrel among themselves, and 7.37 a question about Socrates; the claim turns both into a resolve, “I do not …”, and “with them”, the people who get things wrong, is the object the editor gives to 11.32’s fighting.

support.quote: neither getting idly angry at vice
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about does not get angry at vice to no purpose.
gives: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong
I do not get idly angry at vice

support.quote: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound
support.follows: From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault with people or pounce on them for a slip in their speech.
gives: I do not turn on people for what they get wrong

support.quote: “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”
support.follows: Socrates asks people who say they already have sound souls why, then, they fight and fall out.
gives: I do not fight and fall out with them

claims.t: I take the wide view: of all time and all that exists, and of the things on earth as if from somewhere above. I look round at the courses of the stars and think continually of the elements changing into one another; picturing these things washes away the dirt of life down here on the ground.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of looking at far more than what is in front of me: 7.23 of a mind with “a view of all time and of all being”, 7.26 of looking round at the stars and looking down at the things on earth “as if from somewhere above”.
claims.changed: 7.26 gives instructions; 7.23 describes a mind that has such a view and does not say how to get it. The claim makes one exercise of them. “The wide view” is the editor’s name for what the two describe. 7.26’s list of what is seen from above, from herds to markets, is left out. “Picturing these things” is the translators’ other reading of 7.26’s “the impressions of these things”, and “down here” is added to set the ground against the stars, as the translators’ note does.

support.quote: a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being
support.follows: There is a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of everything that exists.
gives: I take the wide view
of all time and all that exists

support.quote: whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above
support.follows: Anyone who talks about human beings should also look down at earthly things as if from above.
gives: I take the wide view
of the things on earth as if from somewhere above

support.quote: Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.
support.follows: Picturing the stars’ courses and the elements changing into one another washes away the dirt of life on earth.
gives: I take the wide view

claims.t: I shall not be a slave: not to another person’s ignorance, and not as Alexander, Caesar and Pompey were, who had so many things to take thought for and were slaves to so many.
claims.shared: Both passages use the word: 7.37 has “being a slave to anyone’s ignorance”, 8.3 “slavery to how many!” In both it is what marks off the worse soul from the better one.
claims.changed: 8.3 exclaims over the conquerors and gives no instruction, and 7.37 asks whether Socrates was free of it; “I shall not be” is the editor’s turn of both into a resolve. 8.3 does not say whether the conquerors were slaves to things or to people. 8.3c says only “the others”; the names are those 8.3 gives in its first sentence.

support.quote: nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance
support.follows: The soul this passage asks about is not a slave to anyone’s ignorance.
gives: I shall not be a slave
not to another person’s ignorance

support.quote: But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!
support.follows: The others, the three conquerors, had a great many things to take thought for and were slaves to a great many.
gives: I shall not be a slave
not as Alexander, Caesar and Pompey were, who had so many things to take thought for and were slaves to so many

single.quote: Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.
single.label: The mind’s own boundary
single.t: Nature did not blend my mind with my body in such a way that it cannot draw a boundary round itself and bring what is its own under its own control.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It gives a ground for a mind that is not a slave, but it does not use that word and it speaks of the body, so it is not fused with the claim about slavery.
single.follows: The mind is not so mixed with the compound it lives in that it cannot mark itself off and take charge of what is its own.

single.quote: Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
single.label: Bogeys
single.t: When the principles most people live by frighten me, I remember that Socrates used to call them “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
single.why: Only this passage says it, and it does not say which principles are meant. Turning the saying into something I recall when such principles frighten me is the editor’s turn.
single.follows: Socrates called what most people hold and live by “Lamias”, things that frighten children.

single.quote: leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, must consider what comes next: in what way he might live the time he is going to live as well as possible
single.label: The next question
single.t: How long I shall live I leave to god. I consider what comes next: how to live the time I am going to live as well as possible.
single.why: Only this passage turns from how long I live to how well. Socrates puts it guardedly (“perhaps … must”); the item reads that as his polite way of asserting and states it as my resolve, which is the editor’s turn. The trust in “the women who say” that no one escapes what is fated is left out.
single.follows: Perhaps a true man must leave the length of his life to god and ask how to live the time he has as well as possible.

single.quote: not often or without need to say to anyone, or write in a letter, “I am busy”; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that relations with those one lives among call for, by pleading the business that surrounds one
single.label: “I am busy”
single.t: I shall not say or write “I am busy” often or without need, and I shall not keep pleading my business to excuse myself from what I owe the people I live among.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of being busy. 7.37 asks for justice toward people in general; this names one way of failing the people nearest to me.
single.follows: From Alexander the Platonist: seldom to say “I am busy”, and not to plead business to get out of duties to those one lives among.

single.quote: Socrates to Perdiccas, on not going to him: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.
single.label: A kindness I cannot return
single.t: I keep in mind why Socrates would not go to King Perdiccas: so that he would not receive a kindness and be unable to do one in return, which he called the worst of deaths.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of returning a kindness. Marcus gives the saying under a heading and draws no rule from it, so the item keeps it as a reason to remember; “I keep in mind” is the editor’s turn. “King” is from the translators’ note.
single.follows: Socrates would not go to Perdiccas, so as not to receive a kindness he could not return, which he called the worst of deaths.

single.quote: deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression
single.label: Correcting without reproach
single.t: When someone says a thing wrongly, I come out with the right form myself: in my answer, in backing them up, or in talking over the matter itself with them, not the wording.
single.why: Only this passage says how to correct someone. The first half of 1.7 is fused in the claim about other people’s faults; this half is the exercise.
single.follows: From Alexander the grammarian: to correct a slip by deftly using the right form oneself, in an answer or in discussing the matter.

single.quote: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection
single.label: What a tyrant is like
single.t: I keep in mind what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that the people we call patricians are, on the whole, rather lacking in affection.
single.why: Only this passage describes the tyrant and the patricians. Marcus records what he noticed and draws no rule; “I keep in mind” is the editor’s turn. It stands under this label as a picture of what power and high birth can make of a soul, not as a failing of my own.
single.follows: From Fronto: to have noticed what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that patricians are on the whole rather lacking in affection.

single.quote: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.
single.label: The king and the mule driver
single.t: Whichever account of the world is true, Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver came to the same state once they were dead: either both were taken back into the reason that runs the universe, from which all things grow, or both were scattered alike into atoms.
single.why: Only this passage argues by cases, and it is about what death does, not about how to measure a person, so it is not fused with the claim that names Alexander. It says what holds on either account of the world, a universe run by reason or one of atoms only. The item gives the plain sense of the Stoic term “seed-reasons”, as the translators’ note explains it.
single.follows: Once dead, the king and the man who drove his mules were in the same state, whether the universe took them back or they were scattered into atoms.

members.text:
Out of Plato. 'My answer, full of justice and equity, should be
this: Thy speech is not right, O man! if thou supposest that he that is
of any worth at all, should apprehend either life or death, as a matter
of great hazard and danger; and should not make this rather his only
care, to examine his own actions, whether just or unjust: whether
actions of a good, or of a wicked man, &c. For thus in very truth stands
the case, O ye men of Athens. What place or station soever a man either
hath chosen to himself, judging it best for himself; or is by lawful
authority put and settled in, therein do I think (all appearance of
danger notwithstanding) that he should continue, as one who feareth
neither death, nor anything else, so much as he feareth to commit
anything that is vicious and shameful, &c. But, O noble sir, consider
I pray, whether true generosity and true happiness, do not consist in
somewhat else rather, than in the preservation either of our, or other
men's lives. For it is not the part of a man that is a man indeed, to
desire to live long or to make much of his life whilst he liveth: but
rather (he that is such) will in these things wholly refer himself unto
the Gods, and believing that which every woman can tell him, that no man
can escape death; the only thing that he takes thought and care for is
this, that what time he liveth, he may live as well and as virtuously
as he can possibly, &c. To look about, and with the eyes to follow the
course of the stars and planets as though thou wouldst run with them;
and to mind perpetually the several changes of the elements one into
another. For such fancies and imaginations, help much to purge away
the dross and filth of this our earthly life,' &c. That also is a fine
passage of Plato's, where he speaketh of worldly things in these words:
'Thou must also as from some higher place look down, as it were, upon
the things of this world, as flocks, armies, husbandmen's labours,
marriages, divorces, generations, deaths: the tumults of courts and
places of judicatures; desert places; the several nations of barbarians,
public festivals, mournings, fairs, markets.' How all things upon earth
are pell-mell; and how miraculously things contrary one to another,
concur to the beauty and perfection of this universe.
members.english:
“But I would have a just answer to give this man: ‘What you say is not right, fellow, if you think that a man who is of even a little use must take into account the risk of living or dying, rather than look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one.’”

“For this is how it truly is, men of Athens. Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace.”

“But, my dear man, see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life, but, leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, must consider what comes next: in what way he might live the time he is going to live as well as possible.”

Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.

A fine saying of Plato’s. And indeed whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above: herds, armies, farms, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, the din of law courts, empty lands, the varied peoples of the barbarians, festivals, laments, markets, the mixture of every kind and the order put together out of opposites.
members.greek:
ʽἘγὼ δὲ τούτῳ δίκαιον ἂν λόγον ἀντείποιμι, ὅτι οὐ καλῶς λέγεις, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, εἰ οἴει δεῖν κίνδυνον ὑπολογίζεσθαι τοῦ ζῆν ἢ τεθνάναι ἄνδρα, ὅτου τι καὶ σμικρὸν ὄφελος, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐκεῖνο μόνον σκοπεῖν, ὅταν πράττῃ, πότερον δίκαια ἢ ἄδικα πράττει καὶ ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθοῦ ἔργα ἢ κακοῦ.ʼ

Ὁὕτω γὰρ ἔχει, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· οὗ ἄν τις αὑτὸν τάξῃ ἡγησάμενος βέλτιστον εἶναι ἢ ὑπʼ ἄρχοντος ταχθῇ, ἐνταῦθα δεῖ, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, μένοντα κινδυνεύειν, μηδὲν ὑπολογιζόμενον μήτε θάνατον μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν πρὸ τοῦ αἰσχροῦ.ʼ

ʽἈλλʼ, ὦ μακάριε, ὅρα μὴ ἄλλο τι τὸ γενναῖον καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ᾖ τοῦ σῴζειν τε καὶ σῴζεσθαι· μὴ γὰρ τοῦτο μέν, τὸ ζῆν ὁποσονδὴ χρόνον, τόν γε ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄνδρα ἐατέον ἐστὶ καὶ οὐ φιλοψυχητέον, ἀλλ’ ἐπιτρέψαντα περὶ τούτων τῷ θεῷ καὶ πιστεύσαντα ταῖς γυναιξίν, ὅτι τὴν εἱμαρμένην οὐδ’ ἂν εἶς ἐκφύγοι, τὸ ἐπὶ τούτῳ σκεπτέον τίνα ἂν τρόπον τοῦτον ὃν μέλλει χρόνον βιῶναι ὡς ἄριστα βιῴη.ʼ

Περισκοπεῖν ἄστρων δρόμους ὥσπερ συμπεριθέοντα καὶ τὰς τῶν στοιχείων εἰς ἄλληλα μεταβολὰς συνεχῶς ἐννοεῖν· ἀποκαθαίρουσι γὰρ αἱ τούτων φαντασίαι τὸν ῥύπον τοῦ χαμαὶ βίου.

Καλὸν τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος. καὶ δὴ περὶ ἀνθρώπων τοὺς λόγους ποιούμενον ἐπισκοπεῖν δεῖ καὶ τὰ ἐπίγεια ὥσπερ ποθὲν ἄνωθεν κάτω· ἀγέλας, στρατεύματα, γεώργια, γάμους, διαλύσεις, γενέσεις, θανάτους, δικαστηρίων θόρυβον, ἐρήμους χώρας, βαρβάρων ἔθνη ποικίλα, ἑορτάς, θρήνους, ἀγοράς, τὸ παμμιγὲς καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων συγκοσμούμενον.

members.text:
How know we whether Socrates were so eminent indeed, and of so
extraordinary a disposition? For that he died more gloriously, that he
disputed with the Sophists more subtilty; that he watched in the frost
more assiduously; that being commanded to fetch innocent Salaminius, he
refused to do it more generously; all this will not serve. Nor that he
walked in the streets, with much gravity and majesty, as was objected
unto him by his adversaries: which nevertheless a man may well doubt of,
whether it were so or no, or, which above all the rest, if so be that
it were true, a man would well consider of, whether commendable, or
dis-commendable. The thing therefore that we must inquire into, is this;
what manner of soul Socrates had: whether his disposition was such; as
that all that he stood upon, and sought after in this world, was barely
this, that he might ever carry himself justly towards men, and holily
towards the Gods. Neither vexing himself to no purpose at the wickedness
of others, nor yet ever condescending to any man's evil fact, or evil
intentions, through either fear, or engagement of friendship. Whether of
those things that happened unto him by God's appointment, he neither did
wonder at any when it did happen, or thought it intolerable in the trial
of it. And lastly, whether he never did suffer his mind to sympathise
with the senses, and affections of the body. For we must not think that
Nature hath so mixed and tempered it with the body, as that she hath not
power to circumscribe herself, and by herself to intend her own ends and
occasions.
members.english:
How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition? For it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists, and showed more endurance in spending the night out in the frost, and, when ordered to bring in the man from Salamis, was thought to have stood against it more nobly, and “swaggered in the streets”, a point one might well take note of most of all, if indeed it was true. But what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had, and whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods, neither getting idly angry at vice nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance, neither receiving anything allotted from the whole as something foreign or enduring it as something unbearable, nor handing his mind over to feel with the feelings of the poor flesh.

Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.
members.greek:
Πόθεν ἴσμεν, εἰ μὴ Τηλαύγης Σωκράτους τὴν διάθεσιν κρείσσων ἦν; οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ, εἰ Σωκράτης ἐνδοξότερον ἀπέθανε καὶ ἐντρεχέστερον τοῖς σοφισταῖς διελέγετο καὶ καρτερικώτερον ἐν τῷ πάγῳ διενυκτέρευε καὶ τὸν Σαλαμίνιον κελευσθεὶς ἄγειν γεννικώτερον ἔδοξεν ἀντιβῆναι καὶ ʽἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἐβρενθύετοʼ, περὶ οὗ καὶ μάλιστ’ ἄν τις ἐπιστήσειεν, εἴπερ ἀληθὲς ἦν· ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνο δεῖ σκοπεῖν, ποίαν τινὰ τὴν ψυχὴν εἶχε Σωκράτης καὶ εἰ ἐδύνατο ἀρκεῖσθαι τῷ δίκαιος εἶναι τὰ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους καὶ ὅσιος τὰ πρὸς θεούς, μήτε εἰκῇ πρὸς τὴν κακίαν ἀγανακτῶν μηδὲ μὴν δουλεύων τινὸς ἀγνοίᾳ, μήτε τῶν ἀπονεμομένων ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ὡς ξένον τι δεχόμενος ἢ ὡς ἀφόρητον ὑπομένων, μήτε τοῖς τοῦ σαρκιδίου πάθεσιν ἐμπαρέχων συμπαθῆ τὸν νοῦν·

Ἡ φύσις οὐχ οὕτως συνεκέρασε τῷ συγκρίματι, ὡς μὴ ἐφεῖσθαι περιορίζειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ὑφ’ ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖσθαι·

members.text:
Out of Plato. 'He then whose mind is endowed with true
magnanimity, who hath accustomed himself to the contemplation both of
all times, and of all things in general; can this mortal life (thinkest
thou) seem any great matter unto him? It is not possible, answered he.
Then neither will such a one account death a grievous thing? By no
means.'
members.english: “‘So, a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said. ‘Then such a person will count death, too, as nothing terrible?’ ‘Not in the least.’”
members.greek: ʽἯι οὖν ὑπάρχει διανοίᾳ μεγαλοπρέπεια καὶ θεωρία παντὸς μὲν χρόνου, πάσης δὲ οὐσίας, ἆρα οἴει τούτῳ μέγα τι δοκεῖν εἶναι τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον; ἀδύνατον, ἦ δ’ ὅς. οὐκοῦν καὶ θάνατον οὐ δεινόν τι ἡγήσεται ὁ τοιοῦτος; ἥκιστά γε.ʼ

members.text:
What Socrates answered unto Perdiccas, why he did not come unto
him, Lest of all deaths I should die the worst kind of death, said he:
that is, not able to requite the good that hath been done unto me.
members.english: Socrates to Perdiccas, on not going to him: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.
members.greek: Τῷ Περδίκκᾳ ὁ Σωκράτης περὶ τοῦ μὴ ἔρχεσθαι παρ’ αὐτόν· ʽἵνα, ἔφη, μὴ τῷ κακίστῳ ὀλέθρῳ ἀπόλωμαι,ʼ τουτέστι, μὴ εὖ παθῶν οὐ δυνηθῶ ἀντευποιῆσαι.

members.text:
Socrates said, 'What will you have? the souls of
reasonable, or unreasonable creatures? Of reasonable. But what? Of those
whose reason is sound and perfect? or of those whose reason is vitiated
and corrupted? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect. Why then
labour ye not for such? Because we have them already. What then do ye so
strive and contend between you?'
members.english: Socrates used to say: “What do you want? To have the souls of rational beings or of irrational ones?” “Of rational beings.” “Of which rational beings? Sound ones or bad ones?” “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”
members.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγε· τί θέλετε; λογικῶν ψυχὰς ἔχειν ἢ ἀλόγων;—λογικῶν.—τίνων λογικῶν; ὑγιῶν ἢ φαύλων;—ὑγιῶν.—τί οὖν οὐ ζητεῖτε;—ὅτι ἔχομεν.—τί οὖν μάχεσθε καὶ διαφέρεσθε;

members.text:
Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus,
and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all
causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power
and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so
far did their slavery extend.
members.english: And Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates? For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same. But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!
members.greek: Ἀλέξανδρος δὲ καὶ Γάιος καὶ Πομπήιος τί πρὸς Διογένη καὶ Ἡράκλειτον καὶ Σωκράτην; οἱ μὲν γὰρ εἶδον τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὰς αἰτίας καὶ τὰς ὕλας καὶ τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ ἦν αὐτῶν ταὐτά, ἐκεῖ δὲ ὅσων πρόνοια καὶ δουλεία πόσων.

members.text:
Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to
say, or to write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure'; nor in
this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends
and acquaintances (to every one in his kind) under pretence of urgent
affairs.
members.english: From Alexander the Platonist: not often or without need to say to anyone, or write in a letter, “I am busy”; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that relations with those one lives among call for, by pleading the business that surrounds one.
members.greek: Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Πλατωνικοῦ τὸ μὴ πολλάκις μηδὲ χωρὶς ἀνάγκης λέγειν πρός τινα ἢ ἐν ἐπιστολῇ γράφειν ὅτι ἄσχολός εἰμι, μηδὲ διὰ τούτου τοῦ τρόπου συνεχῶς παραιτεῖσθαι τὰ κατὰ τὰς πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας σχέσεις καθήκοντα, προβαλλόμενον τὰ περιεστῶτα πράγματα.

members.why: A note pointing at a story about Socrates in a sheepskin. Marcus does not give what Socrates said, and the story does not survive elsewhere.
members.text:
How Socrates looked, when he was fain to gird himself with a
skin, Xanthippe his wife having taken away his clothes, and carried them
abroad with her, and what he said to his fellows and friends, who were
ashamed; and out of respect to him, did retire themselves when they saw
him thus decked.
members.english: What Socrates was like with the sheepskin tied round his waist, when Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out; and what Socrates said to his companions, who were embarrassed and drew back when they saw him dressed like that.
members.greek: Οἷος ὁ Σωκράτης τὸ κῴδιον ὑπεζωσμένος, ὅτε ἡ Ξανθίππη λαβοῦσα τὸ ἱμάτιον ἔξω προῆλθε, καὶ ἃ εἶπεν ὁ Σωκράτης τοῖς ἑταίροις αἰδεσθεῖσι καὶ ἀναχωρήσασιν, ὅτε αὐτὸν εἶδον οὕτως ἐσταλμένον.

members.text:
Socrates was wont to call the common conceits and opinions of men,
the common bugbears of the world: the proper terror of silly children.
members.english: Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.
members.greek: Σωκράτης καὶ τὰ τῶν πολλῶν δόγματα Λαμίας ἐκάλει, παιδίων δείματα.

members.text:
Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a
tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called
εὐπατρίδαι, _i.e._ nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void
of natural affection.
members.english: From Fronto: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection.
members.greek: Παρὰ Φρόντωνος τὸ ἐπιστῆσαι οἵα ἡ τυραννικὴ βασκανία καὶ ποικιλία καὶ ὑπόκρισις, καὶ ὅτι ὡς ἐπίπαν οἱ καλούμενοι οὗτοι παρ’ ἡμῖν εὐπατρίδαι ἀστοργότεροί πως εἰσί.

members.text:
Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once
dead both came to one. For either they were both resumed into those
original rational essences from whence all things in the world are
propagated; or both after one fashion were scattered into atoms.
members.english: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.
members.greek: Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Μακεδὼν καὶ ὁ ὀρεωκόμος αὐτοῦ ἀποθανόντες εἰς ταὐτὸ κατέστησαν· ἤτοι γὰρ ἀνελήφθησαν εἰς τοὺς αὐτοὺς τοῦ κόσμου σπερματικοὺς λόγους ἢ διεσκεδάσθησαν ὁμοίως εἰς τὰς ἀτόμους.

members.text:
From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not
reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or
any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony,
or confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to
utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and
indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.
members.english: From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound, but deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression, or through some other such well-tuned reminder in passing.
members.greek: Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ γραμματικοῦ τὸ ἀνεπίπληκτον καὶ τὸ μὴ ὀνειδιστικῶς ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι τῶν βάρβαρον ἢ σόλοικόν τι ἢ ἀπηχὲς προενεγκαμένων, ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεξίως αὐτὸ μόνον ἐκεῖνο ὃ ἔδει εἰρῆσθαι προφέρεσθαι ἐν τρόπῳ ἀποκρίσεως ἢ συνεπιμαρτυρήσεως ἢ συνδιαλήψεως περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, οὐχὶ περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος, ἢ δι’ ἑτέρας τινὸς τοιαύτης ἐμμελοῦς παρυπομνήσεως.

members.why: One sentence cut from the end of a chapter: “See what Crates says about Xenocrates.” The saying itself is not given, so there is nothing to build on.
members.text: See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.
members.english: See, at any rate, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.
members.greek: ὅρα γοῦν ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει.

members.why: An example of hosts giving their visitors the better seats. Unlike 11.23 it gives no saying or reason in anyone’s words, and unlike 1.8 Marcus does not name it as something he learned; no other passage of the section speaks of guests.
members.text:
The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint
seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were
content to sit anywhere.
members.english: At their public shows the Spartans used to set the benches for foreign visitors in the shade, while they themselves sat wherever they happened to.
members.greek: Λακεδαιμόνιοι τοῖς μὲν ξένοις ἐν ταῖς θεωρίαις ὑπὸ τῇ σκιᾷ τὰ βάθρα ἐτίθεσαν, αὐτοὶ δὲ οὗ ἔτυχεν, ἐκαθέζοντο.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 7.26 is 7.44–48, 7.37 is 7.66–67a, 7.23 is 7.35, 11.23 is 11.25, 11.32 is 11.39, 1.9 is 1.12, 11.26 is 11.28, 11.21 is 11.23, 1.8 is 1.11, 6.22 is 6.24, 1.7 is 1.10, 6.12 is 6.13b and 11.22 is 11.24; 8.3 is the same.

Takes the words Marcus copied from Plato (the first three paragraphs of 7.26, and all of 7.23) as rules he holds himself. He copies them without comment; “A fine saying of Plato’s” is his only remark.

Reads 7.37’s list as the tests of a soul and uses three of them: just toward people and devout toward the gods, not idly angry at vice, not a slave to anyone’s ignorance. The other two, taking what the whole allots without complaint and not handing the mind over to the body, are left to Articles 3 and 2, which say them.

Calls what 7.37 sets aside “fame” and what the three men of 8.3 stand for “power”. Neither word is in the passages: 7.37 lists what was seen and told of Socrates, and 8.3 only names Alexander, Gaius and Pompey and speaks of their slavery.

Turns two descriptions into resolves: 8.3’s exclamation over the conquerors’ slavery into “I shall not be a slave”, and 7.23’s portrait of a mind with a view of all time into something I practise. Each is marked under the claim as the editor’s turn.
Places 6.22 under “If I doubt it”, as what holds whether the world is governed by reason or is only atoms. It does not say what holds if a person is not to be measured by the soul.

Sets aside three anecdotes that give neither a saying nor a reason: Socrates in the sheepskin (11.26), Crates on Xenocrates (6.12) and the Spartans’ benches (11.22). Socrates and Perdiccas (11.23) is kept because Socrates gives his reason in his own words, and Fronto’s lesson (1.8) because Marcus names it as one.
articles.limit: The section is a collection of sayings and examples, not one argument, and the article leans on two passages: 7.26 feeds three claims and 7.37 four, and claims 1 and 5 rest on the same pair, 7.26 and 7.23, both copied from Plato. Much of it is said in other articles: that I accept what the whole allots (Article 3), that the body’s feelings do not rule me (Article 2), that dying is nothing much and how long I live does not matter (Articles 17 and 35) and that my one fear is of living against nature, not of ceasing to live (Article 10, claim 6, near claim 1 here), that being just is the one thing worth my effort (Articles 10 and 34), that I keep free of anger (Article 37), that I take the wide view, looking down on human affairs from high above and keeping all of eternity and all that exists in mind (Article 10, claim 5, and Article 32, claim 4, the same as claim 5 here; also Article 31), that I look into people’s ruling parts to see what they are (Article 27, claim 1, the same act as claim 2 here), that fame is nothing to me (Article 27), and that the dead are taken back or scattered alike (Articles 32 and 33). What this article adds is the measure of a person, the soul and not fame or power, with the judgment that dying is not the worst thing set beside it.
